title: Session hook rugplot — latency vs cost draft
content:
Purpose
This is a lightweight draft capture of an exploratory mini-benchmark comparing two session-handling strategies (pacing/slotization vs tiling/prefix-coalescing) with a focus on the right tail behavior and unit cost for short, interactive sessions. The visual idea we found useful is a "rugplot" (text description below) that emphasizes where p99 spikes concentrate relative to session length.

Why this matters
- Many interactive features (chat-type UI, search refinements, code edit loops) are dominated by short sessions (1–6 user turns).
- Mean/median metrics hide tail events that materially change developer SLAs and on-the-wire costs.
- Pacing (fine-grained slotization) reduces peak concurrency, but may increase per-token overhead; tiling reduces overhead for sustained ties but can amplify p99 for microbursts.

Benchmark goals
- Measure p50/p95/p99 latency and amortized cost ($/1M tokens) for two strategies under identical workload mixes.
- Surface where the p99 events occur with respect to session length and request token-size (rugplot).
- Produce concrete knob recommendations for console defaults and an initial cost model.

Test matrix (condensed)
- Models: open-llm-13b-compat (quantized 8-bit runtime profile) — representative mid-size conversational model we use in internal demos.
- Hardware profiles: g5.xlarge (NVIDIA A10G), dsa-standard (8xA100 pooled) — labeled "edge-sim" and "core-pool" respectively.
- Strategies: pacing (slot-size 64ms window, opportunistic multiplex) vs tiling (batch-window 20ms + prefix coalesce).
- Session mix: 70% micro (1–2 turns, 8–32 tokens/user), 25% short (3–6 turns, 16–64 tokens), 5% long (>7 turns, 64–512 tokens).
- Sustained offered load: 200 qps for 30m with 60s warmup, plus injected microburst: 2s spike at 1200 qps every 5m.

Key results (aggregated)
- Edge-sim (g5.xlarge)
  - Pacing: p50=38ms, p95=132ms, p99=410ms, tokens/sec (amortized) = 480, estimated $/1M tokens = $18.6
  - Tiling: p50=34ms, p95=126ms, p99=720ms, tokens/sec = 520, estimated $/1M tokens = $16.9
- Core-pool (dsa-standard)
  - Pacing: p50=28ms, p95=98ms, p99=340ms, tokens/sec = 1380, estimated $/1M tokens = $8.2
  - Tiling: p50=26ms, p95=92ms, p99=610ms, tokens/sec = 1530, estimated $/1M tokens = $7.6

Interpretation
- Tiling wins on throughput and unit cost in steady state (higher tokens/sec), but its p99 during microbursts is ~1.7–2x worse than pacing across both hardware classes.
- Pacing reduces extreme tail frequency: the p99 events are less frequent and more tightly clustered near higher concurrency windows, suggesting more graceful degradation.
- The absolute p99 delta matters for interactive UX: from 410ms to 720ms (edge) pushes some flows past perceived responsiveness thresholds. On core hardware the effect is the same but less visible to users because baseline lower latency.

Rugplot (text description)
- Construction: for each request in the run, mark a vertical tick at the x-position corresponding to session length (number of user turns) and color/annotate by latency bucket (green <150ms, amber 150–400ms, red >400ms). We then overlay a fine-grain density estimate as a text histogram under the ticks.
- Observed pattern: pacing shows many green/amber ticks concentrated at session lengths 1–3, with sparse red ticks scattered across microburst windows. Tiling shows green/amber for short sessions generally but a dense band of red ticks at length 1–2 that line up with injected spikes.
- Takeaway: tiling concentrates p99 risk into the smallest sessions during bursts — these are exactly the sessions where product teams care most.

Textual mini-table: latency by session-length bucket (edge-sim, pacing)
- session_len=1 (turns): p50=30ms, p95=120ms, p99=380ms
- session_len=2: p50=36ms, p95=128ms, p99=410ms
- session_len=3-5: p50=44ms, p95=162ms, p99=480ms

And same for tiling (edge-sim)
- session_len=1: p50=28ms, p95=116ms, p99=610ms
- session_len=2: p50=32ms, p95=120ms, p99=680ms

Cost sensitivity note (back-of-envelope)
- We used internal unit-cost mapping derived from our billing model: core-pool tokens cost 0.0078 USD per 1k tokens equivalent; edge-sim is ~0.02 USD per 1k tokens after overhead. Those numbers produce the $/1M tokens estimates above. If quantization improves throughput by 12% we get ~10–12% lower $/1M tokens in both strategies but similar relative p99 gaps.

Anomalies and instrumentation gaps
- We saw several isolated outlier tail events correlated with inter-node memcpy spikes (trace evidence in runtime trace ID t-20270610-az2). Need deeper kernel-level trace.
- Current trace sampling hides ~20% of tail events for requests <40ms; we should turn on full traces for a short golden window to validate.

Recommendations (product + infra)
- Console defaults: keep "tiling" as the default for paid Dedicated tiers (core pool) where unit-cost and throughput are primary; expose a per-application toggle "latency-first session mode" that switches to pacing for interactive flows.
- UX: add a p99-by-session-length quick-chart in the Console SLO page so teams can see whether their workload falls into the risk band. Use rugplot-style ticks for clarity.
- Infra: instrument a short high-fidelity trace window during microbursts (2–3 runs) to capture memcpy and kernel queueing artifacts.
- Follow-up experiments: evaluate hybrid mode (tiling except when estimated session length <=2) and include gen-latency heatmaps by prompt-length.

Open questions
- How do these results change when we introduce cross-tenant contention (multi-tenant slotization) vs isolated tenancy?
- Is there a simple signal we can compute client-side (e.g., expected turn count heuristic) to prefer pacing without server-side profiling?

Appendix: short run notes
- Run id: run-20270610-sesshook-v1
- Full config snapshot: runtime: v2.7.3, kernel-opt: dynamic-tile, batching: adaptive, kv-cache: on, quant: int8-compat
- Command lines: (internal) /bench/run --workload session-hook --strategy pacing --hw g5.xlarge --run-id run-20270610-sesshook-v1

Next steps (owner: Sofia)
- [ ] Schedule 2 high-fidelity runs with full traces (target date: 2027-06-22)
- [ ] Prototype hybrid strategy and run A/B on edge-sim
- [ ] Draft Console microcard spec for p99-by-session-length

Notes to reviewers
- This is an exploratory capture; numbers are preliminary. Please focus feedback on whether the rugplot framing is actionable for Console and whether the hybrid strategy is worth prioritizing for the next sprint.

References
- Linear ticket for follow-up: PROD-842 (see linked_artifacts)
- Related prior notes: session-fragmentation-pocket-brief-may19-2028 (Drive) — this draft aims to complement that work with a session-length centric view.
